title: Central and Southeast Europe Energy Market Outlook 2026 | BloombergNEF
gist: BNEF's outlook for six Central and Southeast European power markets sees solar capacity more than doubling by 2036 (93GW added) while falling realized merchant prices, grid-connection scarcity and coal closures shift value toward batteries, transmission and flexibility. Power price spreads (EUR 118-153/MWh in 2025) are among Europe's highest, but battery merchant returns are warned to erode as deployment grows.

insights.claim: BNEF forecasts 93GW of solar capacity additions from 2026 to 2036 across six Central and Southeast European markets, more than doubling total solar capacity, with Poland, Romania and Bulgaria leading growth.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Large solar pipeline in these markets, but returns depend on location and timing of output rather than volume.
insights.locator: Total solar capacity is set to more than double by 2036

insights.claim: As realized prices for merchant renewable power fall, the value of Contracts for Difference, power purchase agreements and co-location with storage is increasing, and the EU Modernisation Fund financed by ETS revenues is accelerating investment in renewables, storage and grids.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Contracted revenue structures and hybrid solar-plus-storage will command premiums over pure merchant solar.

insights.claim: BNEF expects 20GW of wind additions by 2036, doubling from 21GW installed at the end of 2025, but permitting bottlenecks and limited CfD support constrain deployment.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Wind growth is policy-gated; permitting and CfD design are the variables to watch.
insights.locator: Wind offers a complementary generation profile

insights.claim: Average two-hour day-ahead power price spreads ranged from EUR 118 to 153 per MWh across the six markets in 2025 (EUR 151/MWh in Romania), among the highest in Europe, driven by tight evening supply, inflexible coal generation and solar depressing midday prices.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: High intraday spreads underpin the case for batteries in the region.
insights.locator: Average two-hour day-ahead spreads ranged from

insights.claim: Spreads widened in 2026, partly due to the Iran war's effect on commodity prices, while BNEF estimates a battery coming online in 2026 needs a minimum spread of EUR 85/MWh over the project's lifetime.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Current spreads give headroom over the EUR 85/MWh hurdle, but part of the widening is geopolitical and may not persist.

insights.claim: Merchant battery returns will not necessarily remain good as storage deployment grows; Bulgaria's grant-backed projects total roughly 6-8GW against 7.4GW peak demand in 2025, with about 4GW of batteries already by July 2026, and its fleet is already reshaping regional peak power flows.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Saturation risk: battery arbitrage spreads compress as capacity scales, so avoid underwriting today's spreads.
insights.quote: Merchant returns will not necessarily remain good as storage deployment grows.
insights.locator: Merchant returns will not necessarily remain good

insights.claim: Grid access is becoming one of the region's scarcest assets for project development, and transmission system operators are tightening connection rules through milestones, guarantees, competitive allocation and flexible connections that should release capacity from speculative projects, though connection timing remains a key development risk.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Projects with secured grid connections hold scarcity value; transmission and flexibility assets benefit.
insights.locator: Grid access is becoming one of the region's scarcest assets

insights.claim: Coal still supplied 34% of regional generation in 2025 and is becoming less economic, but security-of-supply concerns are delaying some closures because replacement firm capacity lags.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Coal retirement timelines are likely to slip, prolonging inflexible supply that supports wide spreads.

insights.claim: Gas remains important for adequacy, but rising solar and storage reduce its running hours, making gas plants more dependent on capacity payments and other contracted revenues, while new nuclear largely arrives too late to close the near-term gap.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF
insights.so_what: Gas plant economics hinge on capacity mechanisms rather than energy margins; nuclear does not solve near-term adequacy.
